The user says: "我的分析在哪裡？找到任何包含分析的檔案。" They want to find any file containing "分析" (analysis). So we need to search for files containing that word. Use find? The find tool searches for files or directories containing name. But we need to search for content. There's grep tool to search lines in a file. But we need to find any file containing the word "分析". We could use find to list all files, then grep each. But maybe there's a tool to search for content across files? Not directly. We can use find to get list of files, then grep each. But we can also use grep on each file individually. But we don't know file names. We can use find to list all files. Then iterate. But we can also use grep with pattern "分析" on all files? The grep tool only works on a single file. So we need to find files that contain the word. We can use find to list all files, then grep each. But we can also use find with name pattern "*分析*" but that matches file names containing "分析", not content. The user wants any file containing the word "分析" in content. So we need to search content.

We can use find to list all files, then loop. But we can also use grep on each file. Let's first list all files. Use ls -R? There's no recursive ls. But we can use find to list all files. Use find with path "." and name "*" to get all files. Then we can grep each. But we need to do it programmatically. We can call find with path "." and name "None"? Actually find signature: find(path?: string, name?: string). If name is None, returns all items. So we can call find with path "." and name "None" to get all items. That will return a list of file/directory names. Then we can filter only files. But we don't know which are files vs directories. We can use ls to check. But we can just grep each file. If it's a directory, grep will error. But we can handle errors. But we can just try grep on each file and ignore errors.

Alternatively, we can use grep on each file individually. But we need to know file names. So let's first call find.
